drills.q: Name the three types of distributional shift and state which one necessarily degrades accuracy.
drills.a: Covariate shift (P(X) changes), prior/label shift (P(Y) changes), concept drift (P(Y|X) changes). Only concept drift necessarily degrades accuracy.

drills.q: A feature's PSI comes out to 0.31. What's your read and next step?
drills.a: Above the 0.25 action threshold — investigate. Check whether it correlates with a known event, and check a multivariate/performance signal before deciding to retrain; PSI alone doesn't tell you whether this is concept drift or benign covariate shift.

drills.q: Why would a KS test alert on nearly every window once daily traffic exceeds a few hundred thousand samples?
drills.a: Statistical power scales with sample size; at that scale, even a trivial real difference between two samples produces a near-zero p-value under the null hypothesis of identical distributions.

drills.q: Every univariate PSI/KS check on a feature set passes, but the model is degrading. What technique would you add, and how does it work?
drills.a: A domain classifier: train a model to distinguish reference-window rows from current-window rows using all features jointly. AUC significantly above 0.5 reveals multivariate drift (a changed joint relationship) that no univariate test can see.

drills.q: Your drift monitor uses a rolling 7-day reference window and has never fired despite two years of known gradual model staleness. Explain why, and fix it.
drills.a: A rolling reference absorbs slow drift into its own baseline — each week looks only mildly different from the week before, hiding large cumulative drift. Fix: keep a frozen training-time reference for long-horizon detection alongside the rolling window.

drills.q: Design a retraining trigger policy for a system with a 45-day label lag, avoiding the failure mode of retraining on statistical noise.
drills.a: Use a scheduled floor cadence, gated by a cheap threshold check to skip unnecessary scheduled retrains during quiet periods, escalated to an out-of-cycle retrain only when drift is corroborated by a fast proxy signal (since true labels are too slow) — not on drift alone.

drills.q: Compare PSI and Wasserstein distance on a feature that shifts from bucket [0,10] to [10,20] versus one that shifts to [90,100], with equal proportion of mass moved in both cases.
drills.a: PSI (and KL/JS) report identical drift magnitude in both cases since they only track proportions per bucket. Wasserstein correctly reports the second shift as far more severe because it accounts for how far the actual values moved, not just the proportion.

drills.q: A fixed holdout set shows flat accuracy for months while PSI on three input features climbs steadily. Is this a problem, and what's the one condition that would make it one?
drills.a: Likely covariate shift without concept drift — not an emergency by itself. It becomes a real problem if the fixed holdout itself is stale and no longer represents the current input population, meaning 'flat accuracy on holdout' is measuring the wrong thing.

drills.q: Your retraining pipeline's compute cost rose 30% and leadership asks whether it's worth it. Using this module's concepts, how do you audit it?
drills.a: Check retroactively whether each historical retrain was preceded by drift alone or by drift plus a performance signal. The fraction triggered by drift alone with no subsequent accuracy improvement in the new model is a defensible estimate of wasted spend, pointing to adding a performance-corroboration gate.

drills.q: How do you distinguish gradual drift from a slow seasonal cycle when you only have three months of monitoring history?
drills.a: You often can't reliably from three months alone — you need history spanning at least a full seasonal cycle before concluding 'gradual trend' rather than 'recurring seasonal pattern'; short monitoring windows commonly misdiagnose seasonality as drift.

drills.q: Explain what CBPE-style performance estimation without labels actually computes, and name its key limitation.
drills.a: It estimates accuracy/AUC from the model's own confidence outputs plus observed drift, calibrated against the labeled training/validation distribution. Limitation: it's an estimate that itself degrades under severe or novel drift — exactly the situations where you'd most want to trust it — so it needs periodic validation against real labels once they arrive.
